content: 1. The transdermal system containing norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol is a hormonal contraceptive approved by the FDA for the prevention of pregnancy. 2. WikiDoc does not guarantee the validity of its content and is not a substitute for professional healthcare providers. 3. WikiDoc is intended solely as an educational tool and not for healthcare delivery. 4. The educational content on WikiDoc drug pages is based on FDA package inserts, National Library of Medicine content, and clinical practice guidelines or consensus statements. 5. WikiDoc does not endorse the use of any medication or device in a manner inconsistent with its labeling. 6. The transdermal system has a Black Box Warning, indicating significant risks associated with its use. 7. Common adverse reactions include breast symptoms, nausea/vomiting, headache, application site disorders, abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, menstrual disorders, and mood or anxiety disorders. 8. The transdermal patch is indicated for women who choose this method of contraception, but it may be less effective in women weighing 198 lbs (90 kg) or more. 9. For maximum contraceptive effectiveness, the patch must be used exactly as directed, with detailed instructions available in the FDA-approved patient labeling. 10. The patch follows a 28-day cycle: a new patch is applied weekly for three weeks, followed by a patch-free week during which withdrawal bleeding is expected. 11. Each new patch should be applied on the same day of the week, known as the Patch Change Day. 12. Only one patch should be worn at a time, and it should not be cut, damaged, or altered, as this may impair contraceptive efficacy. 13. After the patch-free week, a new four-week cycle begins with the application of a new patch. The interval between cycles should not exceed seven days. 14. Women starting the patch have two options: First Day Start (apply the first patch within 24 hours of the menstrual period) or Sunday Start (apply the first patch on the first Sunday after the period begins, with backup contraception needed for the first seven days unless the period starts on a Sunday). 15. When switching from oral contraceptives or vaginal rings, the first patch should be applied on the day the next pill or ring would have been started. 16. Postpartum women not breastfeeding should start the patch no sooner than four weeks after childbirth due to an increased risk of thromboembolism. 17. After a first-trimester abortion or miscarriage, the patch may be started immediately without the need for additional contraception. If not started within five days, follow the instructions for first-time users. 18. The patch is contraindicated in women with conditions such as high risk of arterial or venous thrombotic diseases, uncontrolled hypertension, liver disease, breast cancer, or pregnancy. 19. The use of combination hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), particularly during the first year of use, and the risk gradually disappears after discontinuation. 20. Women with a history of cardiovascular disease, smoking, obesity, or family history of VTE should use CHCs with caution. 21. The pharmacokinetic profile of the patch differs from oral contraceptives, with higher steady-state concentrations (Css) and lower peak concentrations (Cmax) of ethinyl estradiol. 22. Women with liver disease, such as acute viral hepatitis or severe cirrhosis, should not use the patch. Discontinue use if jaundice develops. 23. The patch is contraindicated in women with benign or malignant liver tumors, as CHC use is associated with hepatic adenomas and, rarely, hepatocellular carcinoma. 24. Women with uncontrolled hypertension or hypertension with vascular disease should not use the patch. 25. CHC use may slightly increase the risk of gallbladder disease and worsen pre-existing conditions. 26. Women with hypertriglyceridemia or a family history of it may be at increased risk of pancreatitis when using CHCs. 27. If new, recurrent, or severe headaches develop, evaluate the cause and discontinue the patch if indicated. Increased frequency or severity of migraines may indicate a cerebrovascular event. 28. Unscheduled bleeding or spotting may occur with patch use. Rule out malignancy, pathology, or pregnancy if abnormal bleeding persists. 29. Amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea may occur after discontinuing hormonal contraceptives, especially if pre-existing. 30. Extensive studies show no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives before pregnancy or inadvertently during early pregnancy. 31. Women with a history of depression should be carefully monitored, and the patch should be discontinued if depression recurs to a serious degree. 32. The patch is contraindicated in women with current or past breast cancer, as it may be hormonally sensitive. 33. Some studies suggest an association between CHC use and an increased risk of cervical cancer, but this remains controversial. 34. The estrogen component of CHCs may increase serum concentrations of binding globulins, potentially requiring adjustments in thyroid hormone or cortisol therapy. 35. 36. Exogenous estrogens may induce or exacerbate symptoms of hereditary angioedema in susceptible women. 37. Chloasma may occur, particularly in women with a history of chloasma gravidarum. 38. Serious adverse reactions associated with CHC use include cardiovascular events, thromboembolic events, and liver disease. 39. Commonly reported adverse reactions include irregular uterine bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness, and headache.
